title: A mind gone clear
hookLine: not by eye, not by effort: the Mundaka says the self is seen by a mind gone clear, and that's what japa is for
carry: the self is seen by a clear mind
tomorrow: the rivers lose their names in the sea
last: TRUTH ALONE WINS, AND TRUTH IS THE ROAD.

lines: A GLASS OF MUDDY RIVER WATER.
cards: Scoop up a glass of river water after a storm. It's brown and swirling; you can't see a thing through it. Set it on the counter and leave it alone.
Don't filter it, don't stir it. An hour later the mud has settled, and you can see straight through to the other side. Nothing was added.
Something just stopped moving. The Mundaka has spent two chapters on the self. Now it says how the self is seen, and first, how it isn't.

teach.h: NOT BY EYE, NOT BY SPEECH.
teach.b: Angiras's verse starts with a list of no. Na chakshusha grihyate: it isn't grasped by the eye.

Not by speech, not by the other senses, not by austerity, not by works. That's a surprise, because this Upanishad honored austerity and ritual earlier: the rites were called true, and Brahman itself swelled by tapas.
But they're not the hand that grasps it. Then comes the yes. Jnana-prasadena vishuddha-sattvah.
By the clearness of knowledge, the one whose being is purified, meditating, sees it, the one without parts. Prasada means clearness, calm, settling, like water once the mud has sunk.
It can also mean grace and favor, and the same word names the blessed food given out at temples. Here it's knowledge gone clear. Vishuddha-sattva is a being made thoroughly clean.

The self is subtle, known by thought, by a mind in which the five breaths have entered, and the whole mind of creatures is woven through with the senses. When that mind is purified, the self shines out.
So the senses, speech, discipline and ritual aren't thrown away.
They're more like the stirring stick and the filter: useful. But the seeing happens when the water stops moving. And the verse ends with meditating: a mind sitting still long enough to become clear.

Later Vedanta teachers gave this a name, chitta-shuddhi, purifying the mind, and many explain that this is what japa, worship, fasting and service are for: not to grab God, but to let the water settle.

how: In Vedanta teaching, practices like japa, meditation, fasting and worship are often described as ways of purifying the mind (chitta-shuddhi), so that knowledge can arise, rather than as ends in themselves.

o: clearness, a mind settled like still water
a ritual offering poured into the fire
a strict fast that burns away the senses

games.q: how the self is seen — tap the pairs.

s: the Mundaka says the self is grasped by austerity
not by austerity, not by works: by the clearness of knowledge.
prasada can mean clearness and also grace
temple food called prasad shares the word.
the next verse says a purified mind lets the self shine out
when the mind is purified, the self shines forth.

games.q: the self isn't grasped by the eye, by speech, by austerity or by works. what does the Mundaka name instead?
o: the clearness of knowledge, in a mind made pure.
games.why: jnana-prasadena vishuddha-sattvah: by the clearness of knowledge, one whose being is purified, meditating, sees the partless.

practice: Many Hindus do japa: repeating a mantra or a name of God, often on a mala of beads. Om namah Shivaya, or Ram, or simply om. Pick one, or if you don't pray, a word like peace, and repeat it softly.
Don't force the mind still, and don't stir. Each time it wanders, come back to the word, and let the water settle on its own.

wordCard.voice: Prasada, clearness, calm, like water once the mud has settled. In the Mundaka, the self isn't grasped by eye, speech, austerity or works, but by this clearness of knowledge, in a mind made pure.

orig.note: Sanskrit jñāna-prasāda: jñāna, knowledge, + prasāda, clearness, serenity. Mundaka 3.1.8.

carryVoice: Your line: the self is seen by a clear mind. Tomorrow, the rivers reach the sea, and the Mundaka ends. See you then.

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.9 (known by thought; when the mind is purified, the self shines)
